title: Recon and surface mapping
status: AUTHORED. Cheap to do correctly because every driver here is already verified in the manifest.

atom_notes.A08: recon is information exposure from the target's own public surface
atom_notes.A06: names, paths and virtual hosts are namespace structure and the disagreement between layers is the finding
atom_notes.A05: hidden parameters are shape the UI never advertises
atom_notes.A15: version and configuration differences between hosts in the same estate

required_cells.why: passive acquisition costs the target nothing and should precede any active step
turning names into a surface is the pivot every later stage depends on
discovery at scale is the highest yield automated step
deciding what is worth testing is where recon either pays off or drowns you
new hosts and routes appear weekly, which needs monitoring not a one time scan

entries.name: subfinder
entries.role: Passive subdomain enumeration from public sources
preconditions: a root domain and passive sources
oracle: hostnames not visible in any other source
entries.note: Passive first. It costs the target nothing and often finds the forgotten subdomain.

entries.name: dnsx
entries.role: DNS resolution, record types, resolver brute force
oracle: resolved hosts, cname chains and dangling records
entries.note: The -cname plus -a pair is how you find subdomain takeover candidates mechanically.

entries.name: httpx
entries.role: HTTP probing, status, tech detect and titles at scale
oracle: live hosts with status, title and detected technology
entries.note: This is the pivot from names to a surface. Everything downstream consumes its json.

entries.name: naabu
entries.note: Only after httpx. Most web work needs 80/443 and the few adjacent ports, not a full sweep.

entries.name: whatweb
entries.note: Aggression 1 only. Higher aggression is loud and rarely worth it.

entries.name: nmap
entries.role: Service and version truth when HTTP headers lie
entries.note: The fallback arbiter. If httpx and the HTML disagree about the stack, nmap settles it.

entries.name: katana
entries.role: Crawler that executes and parses JS to find endpoints
oracle: endpoint list including routes only JS reveals
entries.note: The -jc flag is the point. A crawler that does not parse JS misses the whole modern surface.

entries.name: gau
entries.role: Known URLs from wayback, commoncrawl and alienvault
entries.note: Free history. Run it before touching the host: it often lists endpoints that were removed from the app but not from the server.

entries.name: ffuf
preconditions: a wordlist and a live host
oracle: status and size clusters revealing hidden paths
entries.note: Set -rate. An agent that ignores rate is a denial of service.

entries.name: feroxbuster
entries.note: Recursion finds the nested app that the flat wordlist misses.

entries.name: gobuster
entries.role: Directory, DNS and vhost brute force
oracle: vhosts or paths that respond differently
entries.note: vhost mode is the underused one: shared IP, different app per Host header.

entries.name: arjun
entries.note: Hidden parameters are where mass assignment and logic bugs start.

entries.name: rea analyze_web_bundle
entries.role: Routes and endpoints from the bundle, which no crawler will find because they are not linked
oracle: route candidates absent from the crawl
entries.note: Crawl finds links. The bundle finds routes. Both are needed and they disagree, which is the interesting part.

entries.name: rea inspect_web_network_capture
entries.role: Endpoint inventory from real traffic, with auth requirement and UI reachability

entries.name: rea capture_browser_scenario
entries.role: Deterministic capture of a scripted flow instead of hand clicking
preconditions: a browser executable or CDP endpoint

entries.name: Shodan and Censys (indexed scan data)
entries.role: What the internet already knows about the estate, with zero requests to the target
preconditions: an authorisation that covers third party data about the target
oracle: hosts and services attributed to the organisation
entries.note: Check the authorisation scope covers querying third party indexes about the target. It usually does not.

tree.q: Is your goal coverage of an estate, or depth on one app?
tree.why: The two goals produce opposite recon strategies and most people run the depth strategy while claiming coverage.

branches.action: passive first, then probe, then fingerprint. never crawl every host, fingerprint and rank instead
branches.oracle: host inventory with technology per host

next.q: Do you have a capture of a real session yet?

branches.action: browse once through the proxy. a capture beats a crawl because it includes authenticated routes
diff three sources: crawl, bundle routes, capture. the set difference is the finding surface
branches.oracle: route present in one source and absent in the others

branches.action: historical urls plus certificate transparency plus dns history, then confirm liveness
branches.oracle: live endpoint absent from current navigation

mirror.detect: dangling cname to an unclaimed service
route present in bundle but never called
mirror.control: inventory from code, not only from traffic
mirror.rule: route in bundle absent in logs

mirror.detect: different app served per Host header on one IP
staging or dev host with weaker auth
mirror.control: same auth posture everywhere, or no public DNS

gaps.gap: No tool diffs crawl, bundle and capture as three sets and reports the differences
gaps.build_candidate: join katana output, rea bundle routes and rea capture urls, emit the three way set difference with source attribution

gaps.gap: No credible ranking of discovered hosts by expected value
gaps.build_candidate: score by tech rarity, auth presence, response novelty and historical change, then sort

gaps.gap: Continuous estate monitoring is a product feature everywhere and a script nowhere
gaps.build_candidate: scheduled httpx diff plus a change feed keyed on title, tech and status
